video_notes.title: RAG at scale: production ready GenAI apps with Azure AI Search
video_notes.contributed: Retrieval-layer scaling mechanics for RAG in production — two-stage recall+rerank, quantization tradeoffs, index density limits, and ingestion pipelines — from the team building Azure AI Search.

video_notes.title: The Multi-Agent Architecture That Actually Ships — Luke Alvoeiro, Factory
video_notes.contributed: A concrete production multi-agent architecture (Factory's 'missions') for long-horizon coding work: orchestrator/worker/validator roles, adversarial validation contracts, serial-not-parallel execution, and per-role model selection.

video_notes.title: The Production AI Playbook: Deploying Agents at Enterprise Scale — Sandipan Bhaumik, Databricks
video_notes.contributed: An end-to-end enterprise playbook (five pillars: evaluation, observability, data foundation, orchestration, governance) grounded in a real banking-chatbot case study with dollar and time figures.

claims.theme: Three ways to add domain knowledge
claims.claim: There are three options for bringing your own domain knowledge to a language model: prompt engineering, fine-tuning (for jargon/patterns), and RAG (for facts the model never saw in training).
claims.quote: for that fine tuning is often a good option

claims.claim: RAG works by separating the reasoning piece (the LLM) from the knowledge piece (an external knowledge base), gluing them together via an orchestration component.
claims.quote: you lean on the language model for the reasoning capabilities

claims.claim: 2023 was the year everyone built RAG prototypes; the 2024 shift is those prototypes going to production, which introduces real concurrent users demanding more data and faster answers.
claims.quote: the interesting shift to this year to 2024 is being these applications are going to production

claims.claim: Going to production stresses RAG systems along five axes at once: data volume, data change rate, query load, workflow complexity (multi-step retrieval+LLM calls), and data source/type diversity.
claims.quote: you end up doing this multi-step workflows that hit the retrieval system and the language model multiple times

claims.claim: Production-grade retrieval uses two stages: a recall-oriented first stage (vectors + keywords) that pulls a large candidate set, then a second-stage rerank with a heavier model on the small candidate set only.
claims.quote: first stage is recall oriented and uses vectors and keywords

claims.theme: Reranking lifts quality across the board
claims.claim: Benchmarked on the same query set, quality ranks BM25 keyword search < vectors-only < fusion (vectors+keywords) < fusion+reranking, with reranking giving a clear step up over fusion alone.
claims.quote: we see better results just out of the box when uh when reranking is enabled

claims.claim: Rerankers are cross-encoder Transformer models that see the query and document together and predict a correspondence label, unlike vector similarity where the model never sees query and document jointly — hence cross-encoders rank higher quality but can't scale to the full corpus.
claims.quote: these type of R rankers are often called cross encoders

claims.claim: Cross-encoder reranking runs at roughly 100ms per query, a deliberate speed/quality tradeoff, and that latency is typically hidden behind the LLM call's own latency in an interactive app.
claims.quote: this is like 100 milliseconds give or take for a model like this

claims.claim: The most effective lever for retrieval quality is narrowing the candidate set with metadata filters before applying ranking tricks — scope first, then rank.
claims.quote: scoping is uh is a very effective way to uh to get quality up

claims.theme: Filters stay cheap at massive scale
claims.claim: Metadata filters (category equals, ranges, AND/OR) remain fast and usable even against hundreds of millions of documents in the index.
claims.quote: even if you have hundreds of millions of documents these are not a problem

claims.theme: Decouple candidate count from returned count
claims.claim: You can request more retrieval candidates than you ultimately return to the LLM (e.g., pull extra from vector and keyword sides, fuse, then rerank down to top-N) — separating recall depth from final answer size.
claims.quote: basically separate how many candidates you want from how many you want to return

claims.claim: Azure AI Search raised vector density limits 10-12x on the same pricing tiers at no extra cost after seeing customers move from tiny indexes to putting all their data in, enabling multi-billion-vector apps on a single provisioned service.
claims.quote: you'll get anywhere 10 between 10 and 12 times the vector density

claims.claim: OpenAI's ChatGPT file uploads and Assistants API vector stores run on Azure AI Search; after Azure raised backend limits, OpenAI increased the limits it gives its own users by 500x.
claims.quote: they increase the limits they give to their users by 500 times

claims.claim: Single-bit vector quantization (float32 to 1 bit, a 32x density gain) still preserves roughly 90-95% of original retrieval precision in evaluations — surprising even to the team that built it — and Cohere independently found ~95% precision retained.
claims.quote: they are still for some models in the mid uh low to mid 90% of the original performance

claims.claim: When Azure AI Search quantizes vectors, it keeps the full-precision originals on the side, so you can query the compressed index for speed and then rerank the retrieved set at full precision to recover the quality lost to compression.
claims.quote: we can do oversampling where we query at the quantized kind compressed version

claims.claim: An integrated-vectorization ingestion pipeline can connect directly to Blob Storage/OneLake/CosmosDB, auto-detect and process only changed data (incremental cost, not a full reindex each time), and handle chunking, vectorization, and format unpacking (PDFs, Office docs, images) as one continuously running pipeline.
claims.quote: we will automatically track changes so it's not a one-hot thing

claims.theme: Combine vector, keyword and metadata in one query
claims.claim: A single retrieval query can combine a vector, free text/keyword search, and categorical filters together, with the engine fusing and ranking the results — avoiding the need to stitch together separate systems.
claims.quote: if I want to combine text and keyword search I can also add search text

claims.theme: Quote-worthy: quality is what users feel
claims.claim: User-perceived quality is directly gated by whether retrieval actually surfaced the pieces of information needed to answer the question — retrieval quality is the ceiling on RAG app quality.
claims.quote: your application works well for your users when they ask a question and they get the answer they're looking for

claims.theme: Attention, not intelligence, is the bottleneck
claims.claim: In software engineering, the bottleneck is no longer model intelligence but human attention: engineers can only drive a couple of the 50 tasks a backlog holds forward per day because every task needs their review.
claims.quote: the bottleneck in software engineering nowadays is not intelligence

claims.claim: A taxonomy of five frontier multi-agent patterns exists: delegation (parent spawns child, waits for a response), creator-verifier (separate fresh agent checks the work), direct communication (agents DM each other, no coordinator), negotiation (agents share a contested resource, ideally net-positive-sum), and broadcast (one agent informs many).
claims.quote: there's five frontier multi-agent frameworks

claims.theme: Direct communication is hard to get right
claims.claim: Direct agent-to-agent communication without a coordinator is hard to get right because state fragments across conversations and there's no single source of truth.
claims.quote: state fragments across conversations without that coordinator

claims.claim: Factory's 'missions' system combines delegation, creator-verifier, broadcast, and negotiation into a single workflow: describe a goal, scope via conversation, approve a plan, then the system executes for hours or days.
claims.quote: combines four of those. Delegation, creator verifier, broadcast and negotiation

claims.claim: Missions uses a three-role architecture: the orchestrator plans and produces a validation contract defining 'done'; workers implement with clean context per feature and commit via Git; validators verify both correctness and end-to-end behavior.
claims.quote: it uses a three-role architecture. There's orchestrator, there's workers and then there's validators

claims.claim: A validation contract is written during planning, before any code exists, defining correctness independently of the implementation; for a complex project this can span hundreds of assertions, and every feature must be covered by at least one.
claims.quote: it's written during planning before any code and it defines correctness independently of implementation

claims.theme: Tests written after code confirm, don't catch
claims.claim: Tests written after implementation are shaped by the code rather than by intent, so they confirm decisions rather than catch bugs — systems relying on post-hoc tests will eventually drift.
claims.quote: tests written after implementation don't catch bugs. They confirm decisions

claims.claim: After each milestone, two validators run: a scrutiny validator (test suite, type checking, lints, plus dedicated code-review agents per feature) and a user-testing validator that spawns the live app and drives it via computer use — filling forms, clicking through flows.
claims.quote: it spawns the application. It interacts with it through computer use

claims.theme: Most wall-clock time is real-world execution
claims.claim: Most of a mission's wall-clock time is spent in the user-testing validator waiting on real-world execution against a live application, not generating tokens.
claims.quote: missions most of the missions wall clock time is actually spent here waiting for this like real world execution

claims.claim: Neither validator has seen the implementation code before, so they aren't invested in it — validation is deliberately adversarial rather than collaborative.
claims.quote: neither validator has seen the code before. They're not invested in the

claims.claim: When a worker finishes, it files a structured handoff detailing what was completed, what was left undone, the commands run and their exit codes, and what issues surfaced — this documentation, not agent memory, is how the system catches problems and self-corrects at milestone boundaries.
claims.quote: not by hoping that agents remember what happened but by forcing them to write it down

claims.claim: Factory's longest mission ran for 16 days — longer than a full sprint — and the team believes missions can run for 30 days given the structure in place.
claims.quote: our longest mission ran for 16 days which is much longer than a full sprint

claims.theme: Parallelism doesn't work for coding agents
claims.claim: Running many coding agents in parallel does not scale throughput in software dev because agents conflict, step on each other's changes, duplicate work, and make inconsistent architectural decisions — coordination overhead eats the speed gains while still burning tokens.
claims.quote: agents conflict. They step on each other's changes. They duplicate work

claims.claim: Missions runs features serially — only one worker or validator active at a time — while parallelizing read-only operations within a feature (code search, API research) and within validators (code review); this looks slower on paper but the error rate drops dramatically over multi-day runs.
claims.quote: it seems slower on paper, but the error rate drops dramatically

claims.claim: Mission Control is a dedicated async monitoring view showing what the active worker is doing, budget burned, and handoff summaries, letting a human act as a supervising project manager instead of a chat participant.
claims.quote: we built mission control, which is a dedicated view for this

claims.claim: No single model is best at every role: planning benefits from slow careful reasoning, implementation from fast code fluency and creativity, and validation from precise instruction-following — matching models to roles ('droid whispering') is a deliberate design skill.
claims.quote: planning benefits from slow, careful reasoning, implementation from fast code fluency and creativity

claims.claim: Validation may deliberately use a different model provider than implementation so that checks aren't biased by the same training data — being locked into one provider constrains you to that family's weakest capability.
claims.quote: validation might use a different model provider entirely to make sure that it's not biased by the same training data

claims.claim: Validation contracts and milestone checkpoints let missions run successfully even with open-weight, non-frontier models, because the process structure — not raw model strength alone — enforces correctness.
claims.quote: they allow you to run missions very very successfully even using open-weight models

claims.claim: In a real mission that built a Slack clone: 60% of time and 60% of tokens went to implementation, validation never succeeded on the first pass (follow-up features were always needed), 50% of final lines of code were tests, and 90% of code was covered by tests.
claims.quote: 60% of our time is spent on implementation, and 60% of our tokens as well

claims.claim: Missions lean heavily on prompt caching to offset the cost of running tasks that span hours or days.
claims.quote: we take advantage of prompt caching heavily to make sure that we're sort of offsetting

claims.theme: Orchestration logic lives in prompts, not code
claims.claim: Almost all of missions' orchestration logic is defined in prompts and skills (about 700 lines of text) rather than a hard-coded state machine, so the system automatically improves with every model upgrade instead of becoming obsolete.
claims.quote: almost all of the orchestration logic is defined in prompts and skills

claims.claim: With missions, a team of five engineers can move from managing roughly 10 concurrent workstreams to roughly 30, freeing them to focus on architecture and product decisions instead of execution.
claims.quote: a team of five engineers might be able to uh work on 10 work streams

claims.claim: The pattern that repeatedly failed: teams pick a model first, build features in a controlled environment with predictable data, get a great-looking demo signed off, then in production nobody can explain why the AI isn't answering the way it did in the demo.
claims.quote: shall we use GPT? Shall we use Claude?

claims.claim: Three recurring gaps sink AI pilots in production: an observability gap (can't trace what the AI actually did), an evaluation gap (no defined metric that matters to the business, measured continuously), and a governance gap (no accountability for failures).
claims.quote: the first one is the observability gap

claims.claim: The production framework has five pillars to address before/while building: evaluation, observability, data foundation, orchestration, and governance — ideally in sequence, though real projects rarely follow it cleanly.
claims.quote: these are the five pillars

claims.claim: Evaluation is the specification for an AI system: define success in numbers (accuracy target, tolerable false-positive rate, deflection rate) before writing any code or discussing models.
claims.quote: evaluation is basically specification for your AI system

claims.theme: Build the golden dataset from real experts
claims.claim: Build the evaluation/golden dataset by talking to domain experts about what real human agents actually answer, including gray-area and edge-case questions, then automate a pipeline that scores live responses against it continuously.
claims.quote: talk with the domain experts and find what is actually happening in real life on the ground

claims.claim: Evaluation architecture has three layers: deterministic checks (formats, regex, classic NER/PII models — cheap, do first), non-deterministic semantic checks (LLM-as-judge for groundedness, safety, relevance), and behavioral checks (are tool calls correct, duplicated, or looping).
claims.quote: the first layer is deterministic

claims.theme: Behavioral evals catch expensive hidden bugs
claims.claim: An agent can give a correct answer while making three redundant database calls to get there — invisible in a demo, but an expensive, easy-to-miss problem at thousands of queries a day; behavioral evaluation is the layer most teams skip.
claims.quote: the agent uh actually made three calls to the database to find that answer

claims.theme: Tracing a real dispute end to end
claims.claim: In a banking chatbot, one user request (waive an overdraft fee) traced through intent classification, an account-database API call, a RAG lookup of policy documents, a reasoning step, and a final guardrail check — this is the level of detail full tracing should capture.
claims.quote: it retrieves policy documents. It checks from a rag vector database

claims.claim: Without tracing in place, a team facing a customer dispute over an AI decision has no way to reconstruct what happened and typically defaults to just giving the customer a discount to placate them.
claims.quote: you have no way to check what the AI did

claims.claim: With online monitoring in place, detected failures (like duplicate or failing API calls) can trigger fallback strategies automatically, e.g., retry up to three times then escalate to a human.
claims.quote: go and retry for three times, not more than three times

claims.theme: Data foundation eats 60% of project time
claims.claim: Data foundation work — split into 'question data' (serving/answering data) and 'tracking data' (tracing/observability) — typically consumes about 60% of project time, because agents (unlike humans) act confidently on bad data instead of catching and correcting it.
claims.quote: I spend 60% of my time, uh and I see I see a lot of organizations spending a lot of time here

claims.claim: Data was always built for humans, who are forgiving of errors and correct them in-line; agents are not forgiving — they will confidently give a wrong answer from bad data without flagging it.
claims.quote: agents will go, find it wrong, they'll give you the wrong answer confidently

claims.claim: The Databricks stack for a production data foundation layers as: cloud storage (raw files) -> Delta Lake (table-like structure via manifest files, incremental loading) -> Unity Catalog (centralized permissions, metadata/PII tagging, discovery) -> application layer (Mosaic AI, Genie text-to-SQL, Agent Bricks).
claims.quote: we help you create this um you know, uh table-like structure on top of it using manifest files

claims.claim: Three orchestration patterns fit different needs: orchestrator-worker (central control, every request logged through the orchestrator, easy to debug), choreography (independent agents listening to a shared message bus, run in parallel, lower latency since there's no central round-trip), and human-in-the-loop (a human is pulled in when confidence drops below a threshold).
claims.quote: the first one I describe here is the orchestrator worker pattern

claims.claim: In the choreography pattern, agents run in parallel and are not dependent on an orchestrator relaying messages back and forth, which reduces latency compared to centrally coordinated patterns.
claims.quote: the advantage it brings you is the latency is reduced because they are not dependent on an orchestrator

claims.claim: Applying NER-based PII pre-validation during testing caught 47 PII breaches before the system went to production.
claims.quote: we already detected 47 PII breaches during the testing phase

claims.claim: Prompt versioning must be treated as enterprise change management, not a casual git commit — every prompt change needs the same governance rigor as a code change.
claims.quote: you have to treat prompt versioning as change management in enterprise grade solution

claims.claim: When model providers upgrade their models, don't trust published benchmark boards — rerun the upgraded model against your own evaluation dataset before switching, and keep the flexibility to use more than one model provider as a risk hedge.
claims.quote: you cannot really rely on one single model

claims.claim: Before this framework was applied, a retail banking client spent roughly $85K over 6 months on a chatbot POC that did not succeed, with no one able to explain why it failed in production.
claims.quote: they spent around 85K in 6 months doing a POC which did not succeed

claims.theme: Model selection deferred to week 7 of 8
claims.claim: In the redo of the banking chatbot project, the team deliberately delayed model selection to week 7 of an 8-week POC, spending weeks one and two building the evaluation layer first — inverting the typical 'pick a model first' order.
claims.quote: we selected the model in week seven, like in a eight weeks POC

claims.claim: The banking chatbot's success criteria were defined in hard numbers: handle 60% of user queries (the simple ones), hit about 85% accuracy, plus latency and other operational targets — not vague notions of 'good.'
claims.quote: they needed some sort of accuracy. So, 85% it was around 85% accuracy target

claims.theme: Eval dataset is a living system
claims.claim: The evaluation dataset should start small (this case started at 200 real agent-answered cases) and grow continuously as new failures are found and added — treating it as a living system, not a one-time artifact.
claims.quote: your evaluation data set is a living system

claims.theme: Stale embeddings caused a live incident
claims.claim: A real production incident: after the bank updated an interest-rate policy, the new policy document never made it into the vector database (embeddings didn't update), so the chatbot kept giving stale answers — caught via a CSAT/thumbs-down drop and trace inspection, not by anyone flagging the data pipeline directly.
claims.quote: the new policy document was not updated in the vector database. The embeddings did not come through

claims.claim: A production incident playbook should follow: detect (via the eval dashboard) -> diagnose (via tracing) -> contain (roll back/version the prompt, or apply fault-tolerance patterns like saga, compensation, or circuit breaker) -> fix (using the test case library and LLM-judge reports) -> add the case to the eval suite so it's caught automatically next time.
claims.quote: first, you detect using your eval dashboard. Then you diagnose using your tracing

claims.theme: Cap expensive layer-3 eval runs in CI
claims.claim: Behavioral (layer-3) evals get expensive to rerun at scale (300-500+ rows) as the eval set grows, so run only a small subset on each CI change and reserve the full eval suite for merges to main to control cost.
claims.quote: you only do the full test when you merge to the main branch

disagreements.topic: Whether running multiple agents in parallel is a good production strategy

positions.position: For software-dev tasks specifically, parallel agents conflict, duplicate work, and produce inconsistent architectural decisions; Factory's missions deliberately run features serially (one worker/validator at a time) with only read-only sub-steps parallelized, because correctness compounds over multi-day runs.

The choreography orchestration pattern runs independent agents in parallel against a shared message bus (e.g., separate agents pulling customer details and approval details for a mortgage application) and presents this as advantageous, reducing latency because agents aren't waiting on a central orchestrator.

gaps: None of the three talks give concrete dollar or token-cost figures for running retrieval/rerank infrastructure or multi-agent missions at steady-state production volume (Factory mentions prompt caching helps, but not by how much; Azure talk gives no pricing).

The Databricks talk shows a vector database going stale (policy doc embeddings not refreshed) as a real incident, but none of the three videos describe a concrete freshness/refresh strategy (e.g., cadence, staleness alarms) to prevent this proactively rather than detect it after CSAT drops.
No talk addresses how to choose which specific cross-encoder or reranker model to deploy beyond citing Azure's ~100ms budget — no comparative guidance on reranker model selection.
Factory's talk does not explain how the hundreds of assertions in a validation contract are authored, reviewed, or kept from becoming stale as requirements change over a 16-30 day mission.
None of the talks detail concrete prompt-injection or adversarial-input defenses for agents that call external tools/APIs in production, beyond generic mentions of guardrail checks and PII detection.

The Azure AI Search talk does not address multi-agent orchestration at all, and the two agent-orchestration talks (Factory, Databricks) do not address vector index scaling/quantization — a reader wanting both retrieval-infra scaling and agent-orchestration scaling has to synthesize across talks with no single source of truth on how they interact (e.g., how RAG retrieval scaling interacts with multi-agent tool calls).
